title: Building an Internal Automation Platform
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Building an Internal Automation Platform ##### From bottleneck to platform An automation engineer at a 200-person company became a queue. Marketing wanted a lead router, finance wanted invoice processing, support wanted ticket triage, and ops wanted three reports. Every request went through one person, and the backlog stretched to eleven weeks. Meanwhile, four teams had quietly built their own Zapier accounts on departmental credit cards. Nobody knew what those automations did, what credentials they held, or what would break when the people who built them left. Both failures come from the same root: **there was no platform**. There was a person doing projects, and shadow IT filling the gap. The shift that fixes it is treating automation as a **product other teams consume** — with paved roads, guardrails, self-service, and governance — rather than a service one person performs. ##### Platform versus project mindset | | Project mindset | Platform mindset | |---|---|---| | Unit of work | One automation for one team | Reusable capabilities for all teams | | Success measure | Automations delivered | Teams enabled, time-to-first-automation | | Your role | Builder | Enabler, reviewer, capability owner | | Scaling | Hire more builders | Improve self-service | | Governance | Ad hoc | Built into the paved road | The organizing concept is the **paved road** (or golden path): the well-supported, documented, secure way to do a common thing. Teams may leave the paved road, but then they own the consequences — support, security review, on-call. Most choose the road, because it is genuinely easier. Concretely, a paved road means: a template for the common workflow shape, pre-approved credentials, a shared error-handling and logging sub-workflow, a dev environment, a review checklist, and documentation that answers the first five questions anyone asks. ##### Platform architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph SS["Self-service layer"] T[Template library] --> D[Dev environment] D --> R[Review + promote] end subgraph CORE["Platform core"] N[n8n queue mode
dev / staging / prod] TEMP[Temporal
long-running processes] API[Shared FastAPI services
RAG · validation · enrichment] end subgraph SHARED["Shared services"] V[(Vault
credentials + RBAC)] PG[(PostgreSQL
state + audit + usage)] RQ[(Redis
queues + cache)] OBS[Prometheus · Grafana
Loki · Langfuse] end R --> N N --> TEMP & API N & TEMP & API --> V & PG & RQ N & TEMP & API --> OBS OBS --> CB[Cost showback
per team] ``` The core decision is which capabilities are **shared** rather than rebuilt per team. The list that pays for itself: credential management, error handling and alerting, logging and run history, notification formatting, deduplication, canonical schema mapping, AI/RAG access, and cost tracking. Every one of those, implemented eleven times by eleven teams, is eleven times the maintenance and eleven inconsistent behaviours. ##### Credentials and RBAC The shadow-IT problem is fundamentally a credentials problem: teams built their own automations because they could not get access through you. The platform answer is **delegated, scoped access** — teams manage their own connections within boundaries the platform enforces. ```hcl # Vault policy: the marketing team can read only their own secrets path "secret/data/teams/marketing/*" { capabilities = ["read", "list"] } path "secret/data/shared/read-only/*" { capabilities = ["read"] } path "secret/data/teams/finance/*" { capabilities = ["deny"] # explicit deny beats accidental grant } ``` Layer this with n8n's project and role model — projects per team, credentials scoped to a project, roles distinguishing who can edit versus merely execute — and with per-workload service accounts holding least-privilege scopes. Three rules that prevent the audit problem from the story: **one credential per team per integration** (never shared across teams), **rotation with a documented owner**, and **an inventory** mapping credential → owner → consuming workflows → last rotation. ##### Templates and a component library Templates are how you make the paved road faster than the alternative. **Workflow templates** — a starting point with error handling, logging and structure already wired: ```text templates/ ├── 01-webhook-to-crm/ verify → dedupe → validate → map → upsert → log ├── 02-scheduled-report/ cron → query → format → deliver → log ├── 03-ai-classification/ input → LLM (schema) → validate → confidence gate → route ├── 04-approval-workflow/ trigger → Slack card → wait → act → audit └── 05-bulk-sync/ watermark → paginate → transform → upsert → advance ``` **Reusable sub-workflows** are the components, and these matter more than templates because they stay linked: - `common/handle-error` — classify, retry, dead-letter, alert by severity. - `common/log-run` — write to the platform's run table with standard fields. - `common/notify` — severity-aware Slack/email formatting. - `common/dedupe-check` — idempotency against the shared store. - `common/canonical-contact` — map any source into the canonical schema. - `common/ai-classify` — schema-validated LLM call with confidence and cost logging. Publish each with a documented interface — inputs, outputs, failure modes — so a consuming team can use it without reading its implementation. The payoff is concrete: when you improve error classification, thirty workflows improve at once. ##### Environments and promotion ```text DEV teams build freely · test credentials · test destinations · no approval STAGING production-shaped · anonymized data · automated tests run here PROD change requires review + approval · full monitoring · on-call coverage ``` n8n's Git-backed **Source Control** makes promotion a pull request: push from dev to a branch, review the workflow diff, merge, pull into production. That single mechanism gives you version history, review, rollback and an audit trail — the four things ad-hoc copying lacks. ```yaml # .github/workflows/promote.yml — production promotion with a gate on: push: { branches: [main], paths: ["workflows/**"] } jobs: validate: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Scan exported workflows for embedded credentials run: | if grep -rEi '"(api[_-]?key|token|password|secret)"\s*:\s*"[^"]{12,}"' workflows/; then echo "::error::Credential found in workflow JSON"; exit 1 fi - name: Enforce naming convention run: python scripts/check_naming.py workflows/ - name: Require owner + description metadata run: python scripts/check_metadata.py workflows/ promote: needs: validate environment: production # required reviewer configured here runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: python scripts/import_workflows.py --env prod env: N8N_URL: ${{ secrets.N8N_PROD_URL }} N8N_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.N8N_PROD_KEY }} ``` ##### Governance without bureaucracy Governance fails when it is heavier than the workaround. Keep it proportionate to risk. **Intake** — a short form, not a committee. What process, what systems, what volume, does it touch PII or money, who owns it afterwards, what should improve and by how much. Ten fields, answered in five minutes, and the answers determine the review tier. **Tiered review:** | Tier | Criteria | Review | |---|---|---| | **Self-serve** | Internal data, no PII, no writes to systems of record | None — template + platform guardrails | | **Light** | Writes to a business system, moderate volume | Async checklist review, one platform engineer | | **Full** | PII, money, customer-facing, or high volume | Design review, security sign-off, staged rollout | Most requests land in the first two tiers, which is what keeps the platform team from becoming the bottleneck again. **Naming convention** — enforced by CI so it is never a debate: ```text [team]-[system]-[purpose]-[trigger] marketing-hubspot-lead-routing-webhook finance-tally-invoice-sync-cron-0200 support-zendesk-ai-triage-webhook [TEST] prefix for anything non-production ``` **Review checklist** — the same questions every time: named owner and description present; credentials from the vault, not inline; error handling and alerting wired; idempotent writes; PII documented and minimized; run logging in place; naming and tagging correct; documented in the catalogue; cost estimated. **A workflow catalogue** — auto-generated from workflow metadata into a searchable page. This is what makes "who owns this and what does it touch?" answerable, and it directly solves the shadow-IT visibility problem. ##### Cost showback and platform metrics Attribute cost to teams and the conversation changes from "the platform is expensive" to "marketing's enrichment workflow costs ₹14,000/month — is that worth it?" ```sql -- Monthly platform cost by team, with the drivers broken out SELECT team, COUNT(*) AS executions, ROUND(SUM(llm_cost_usd) * 84, 2) AS ai_cost_inr, ROUND(SUM(external_api_cost_usd) * 84, 2) AS api_cost_inr, ROUND(SUM(compute_seconds) / 3600.0 * INFRA_RATE_INR, 2) AS compute_inr, ROUND(100.0 * AVG((status = 'success')::int), 1) AS success_rate, ROUND(SUM(minutes_saved) / 60.0, 1) AS hours_saved FROM platform_runs WHERE started_at >= date_trunc('month', now()) GROUP BY team ORDER BY (SUM(llm_cost_usd) + SUM(external_api_cost_usd)) DESC; ``` **Showback** (visibility only) is the right starting point; **chargeback** (actual budget transfer) creates real incentives but also real friction — introduce it only once the numbers are trusted. The platform's own health metrics are different from any individual workflow's: **time-to-first-automation** for a new team, **percentage of automations built without platform-team involvement** (the self-service ratio), **template adoption rate**, **platform uptime**, **total hours saved across the organization**, and **shadow-IT instances discovered**. Those numbers are what justify the platform's existence at budget time. ##### Common pitfalls - **Building a platform nobody asked for** — start from three real teams' needs, not an architecture diagram. - **Governance heavier than the workaround**, which recreates shadow IT. - **No self-service**, leaving the platform team as the bottleneck. - **Templates that are copies rather than linked sub-workflows**, so improvements do not propagate. - **No dev environment**, forcing people to test in production. - **Shared credentials across teams**, destroying attribution and blast-radius control. - **No workflow catalogue** — unowned automations accumulate. - **Cost invisible to consumers**, so nobody optimizes. - **Sub-workflows without documented interfaces**, which nobody trusts enough to reuse. - **No deprecation process** for automations whose owners have left. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: stand up an internal n8n platform with a **template library, shared vault, RBAC, and dev/prod environments**, then write the **governance model** — intake, review checklist, naming convention, cost showback. Build at least three of the shared sub-workflows (`handle-error`, `log-run`, `notify`) and use them in two different workflows, because the reuse is what makes it a platform rather than a shared login. The mini project is that platform made genuinely self-serviceable: another team should be able to go from idea to a running dev workflow **without you**. Test it literally — hand a colleague the documentation and a template, and time how long it takes them and where they get stuck. Every place they stall is a gap in the paved road, and fixing those is the actual work of a platform team. For the assignment, write the **governance model**: intake form, review checklist, naming convention, and a cost showback report. Keep the intake to ten fields and the checklist to nine items, and define the tiering explicitly — which requests need no review, which need an async checklist, which need a design review. Governance that people can complete in five minutes is governance they will actually follow. ##### Key takeaways - Shift from delivering projects to enabling teams: paved roads with templates, shared services and guardrails scale where a single builder cannot. - Share the capabilities everyone needs — credentials, error handling, logging, notifications, dedup, canonical mapping, AI access — as linked sub-workflows, not copied snippets. - Delegate credential access with scoped vault policies and per-team projects; shadow IT is usually a symptom of blocked access. - Promote through dev → staging → prod with Git-backed source control, CI validation and an approval gate, so every production change is reviewed and reversible. - Keep governance proportionate with tiered review, enforce naming in CI, maintain a workflow catalogue, and make cost visible per team so optimization has an owner.
